text:
Dear Dr. Mercer,

Thank you for seeing Leo, an eight-year-old boy who recently presented for evaluation following several weeks of general malaise. He lives at home with his parents and younger sister, and his past medical and family histories are non-contributory.

On examination, Leo is interactive and attentive, showing no drowsiness. His cranial nerves are intact. Motor testing revealed full strength throughout, with no upper limb weakness and no hemiplegia. Abdominal palpation, however, is notable for significant visceral enlargement: his liver edge is firm and palpable 4 cm beneath the right costal margin, and splenomegaly is readily detectable 3 cm below the left costal margin. 

Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated pancytopenia, with concurrent anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Hepatic panels show elevated transaminases, with an AST of 172 U/L and an ALT of 195 U/L, alongside a pronounced rise in serum LDH. Ferritin levels are also strikingly high at over 3,500 ng/mL. His renal profile was unremarkable, and circulating copper concentrations were entirely normal.

Given his systemic presentation, we arranged neuroimaging. A brain MRI demonstrated patchy, confluent areas of high signal intensity involving the cerebral white matter on T2 and FLAIR sequences; notably, the radiologist confirmed there was no evidence of central nervous system demyelination. 

In light of his marked organomegaly, multilineage cytopenias, transaminitis, raised ferritin, and cerebral white matter signal abnormalities, I would greatly value your comprehensive assessment and recommendations regarding the next steps in his diagnostic workup.

Sincerely,
Dr. Evelyn Vance
